prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) -- Some of Zimbabwe's children are "wasting away" as political turmoil and economic crisis have caused a severe food shortage, according to a report from Save the Children. Children sleep in rough conditions on the border between Zimbabwe and South Africa. The number of acute child malnutrition cases has risen by almost two-thirds in the past year, the report from the UK-based agency said in its appeal to world donors for help. "There is no excuse for failing to provide this food," program director Lynn Walker said. "The innocent people of Zimbabwe should not be made to suffer for a political situation that is out of their control." Five million Zimbabweans -- out of a population of about 12 million -- are in need of food aid now, the report said. The group is appealing for 18,000 tons of food for next month. "We have already been forced to reduce the rations of emergency food we are delivering because there isn't enough to go around," the report said. "If, as we fear, the food aid pipeline into Zimbabwe begins to fail in the new year the millions of people who rely on emergency food aid will suffer." Zimbabwe is facing its worst economic and humanitarian crisis since its independence from Great Britain 28 years ago. There is an acute shortage of all essentials such as cash, fuel, medical drugs, electricity and food. President Robert Mugabe blames the crisis on the sanctions imposed on him and his cronies by the West for allegedly disregarding human rights. But Mugabe's critics attribute the crisis to his economic policies. As the economy has faltered for almost a decade now, a cholera epidemic is raging, fueled by the collapse of health, sanitation and water services in Zimbabwe. The epidemic has claimed more than 1,100 lives and infected more than 20,000 people since its outbreak in August. Health experts have warned that the water-borne disease could infect more than 60,000 unless its spread is halted. The political crisis rose to a boil in this year when the opposition party claimed that it won the presidential election, but Mugabe's government refused to recognize the result. Instead, the race was thrown to a runoff, which was boycotted by the opposition. Mugabe signed an agreement with the opposition in September to form a unity government, but a bitter dispute over the division of cabinet seats has prevented its formation. Inflation is so severe that the government was forced to print $10 billion currency notes last week, with each expected to buy just 20 loaves of bread.

Children are sleeping in harsh conditions along the border between Zimbabwe and South Africa. Cases of acute child malnutrition have risen by nearly two-thirds over the past year, the UK-based agency said in an appeal to international donors for assistance.

“There is no excuse for failing to provide this food,” said Lynn Walker, the organization’s program director. “The innocent people of Zimbabwe should not be made to suffer for a political situation that is out of their control.”

Five million Zimbabweans — out of a population of about 12 million — are currently in need of food aid, the report said. The organization is appealing for 18,000 tons of food for next month.

“We have already been forced to reduce the rations of emergency food we are delivering because there isn’t enough to go around,” the report said. “If, as we fear, the food aid pipeline into Zimbabwe begins to fail in the new year, the millions of people who rely on emergency food aid will suffer.”

Zimbabwe is facing its worst economic and humanitarian crisis since gaining independence from Great Britain 28 years ago. The country is experiencing acute shortages of essential goods and services, including cash, fuel, medical drugs, electricity and food.

President Robert Mugabe blames the crisis on sanctions imposed by the West on him and his associates over alleged human rights abuses. His critics, however, attribute the crisis to his economic policies.

As the economy has faltered for nearly a decade, a cholera epidemic has raged, fueled by the collapse of Zimbabwe’s health, sanitation and water services. The outbreak has claimed more than 1,100 lives and infected more than 20,000 people since it began in August. Health experts have warned that the water-borne disease could infect more than 60,000 people unless its spread is contained.

The political crisis reached a boiling point this year when the opposition party claimed victory in the presidential election, but Mugabe’s government refused to recognize the result. Instead, the election proceeded to a runoff, which the opposition boycotted.

Mugabe signed an agreement with the opposition in September to form a unity government, but a bitter dispute over the allocation of Cabinet seats has prevented its formation.

Inflation is so severe that the government was forced last week to print $10 billion currency notes, each expected to buy only 20 loaves of bread.

Zimbabwe is experiencing its most severe economic and humanitarian emergency since gaining independence from Britain 28 years ago. Basic necessities are in critically short supply, including money, fuel, medicines, electricity and food.

President Robert Mugabe says the crisis is the result of Western sanctions placed on him and his associates over alleged human rights abuses. His opponents, however, argue that the disaster stems from his government’s economic decisions.

As Zimbabwe’s economy has deteriorated over nearly 10 years, a cholera outbreak has intensified, worsened by the breakdown of the country’s health care, sanitation and water systems. Since the epidemic began in August, more than 1,100 people have died and over 20,000 have been infected. Medical specialists have cautioned that more than 60,000 people could contract the waterborne illness if it is not contained.

In September, Mugabe reached a deal with the opposition to create a unity government, but the plan has not been implemented because of a fierce disagreement over how cabinet posts should be shared.

Inflation has reached such an extreme level that the government had to issue $10 billion banknotes last week, with each note expected to be worth only about 20 loaves of bread.

counterfactuals.output:
**Harare, Zimbabwe** — Save the Children is warning that Zimbabwean children are facing acute malnutrition as the country’s prolonged political and economic crisis deepens, leaving families struggling to afford food, health care and other basic needs.

The aid organization says many households are being pushed to the brink by soaring prices, unemployment, food shortages and limited access to essential services. In some communities, parents are cutting back on meals, withdrawing children from school, or relying on unsafe coping measures to survive.

Health workers and humanitarian groups say children are among the hardest hit. Acute malnutrition can develop quickly when a child does not get enough nutritious food or suffers repeated illness, and it can become life-threatening without urgent treatment. Young children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers are considered especially vulnerable.

Zimbabwe has faced years of economic instability, marked by high inflation, currency volatility and shortages of key goods. The crisis has been compounded by drought conditions in parts of the country, poor harvests and the rising cost of imported food and fuel.

Save the Children is calling for increased humanitarian support to help provide food assistance, nutrition treatment, clean water and health services. The organization is also urging authorities and international donors to prioritize children in emergency response plans.

Families in the capital, Harare, and in rural areas say even basic staples such as maize meal, cooking oil and vegetables have become increasingly difficult to buy. For many, wages have failed to keep pace with price increases, forcing households to make impossible choices between food, school fees and medical care.

Aid agencies warn that without swift action, the number of children suffering from malnutrition could rise further, with long-term consequences for their health, development and education.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an article on Zimbabwe’s humanitarian crisis in 2008, including food shortages, child malnutrition, cholera deaths, hyperinflation, and the political standoff between Robert Mugabe and the opposition.
counterfactuals.output:
# Zimbabwe’s 2008 Humanitarian Crisis: Hunger, Disease, Hyperinflation and Political Deadlock

In 2008, Zimbabwe faced one of the gravest humanitarian crises in its post-independence history. A convergence of food shortages, economic collapse, political violence, and a devastating cholera epidemic left millions of people struggling to survive. The crisis unfolded against the backdrop of a bitter political standoff between President Robert Mugabe and the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), deepening instability and delaying effective responses to urgent human needs.

## A Nation Facing Hunger

By 2008, Zimbabwe’s agricultural sector had been severely weakened by years of economic mismanagement, controversial land reforms, shortages of seed and fertilizer, drought conditions in some areas, and the collapse of rural infrastructure. Once regarded as a regional breadbasket, the country became heavily dependent on food aid.

Millions of Zimbabweans faced serious food shortages. Staple foods such as maize meal, cooking oil, and bread became scarce or unaffordable. Many families reduced their meals to once a day, while others survived on wild fruits, roots, or assistance from relatives and humanitarian agencies. In both rural and urban areas, food insecurity became a daily reality.

International agencies warned that large portions of the population required emergency food assistance. However, aid distribution was complicated by political tensions, restrictions on humanitarian organizations, and allegations that food aid was sometimes manipulated for political purposes.

## Child Malnutrition and a Collapsing Health System

Children were among the most vulnerable victims of the crisis. As household food supplies dwindled and parents lost income, malnutrition increased. Clinics and hospitals reported rising numbers of undernourished children, including cases of severe wasting and stunting.

The health system, already under strain, was close to collapse. Hospitals lacked basic medicines, equipment, clean water, and functioning sanitation. Many doctors and nurses had left the country in search of better pay, while those who remained often could not afford transportation to work because their salaries had been destroyed by inflation.

For malnourished children, this collapse was especially dangerous. Illnesses that might have been treatable—diarrhea, respiratory infections, malaria, and measles—became life-threatening when combined with hunger and lack of medical care.

## Cholera Outbreak and Thousands of Deaths

In late 2008, Zimbabwe was struck by a major cholera outbreak, one of the most visible symbols of the country’s deteriorating public services. Cholera, a waterborne disease, spread rapidly in areas where clean water systems had failed and sewage infrastructure had broken down.

Urban centers such as Harare were severely affected, but the outbreak also spread to rural districts and across borders into neighboring countries. Burst sewage pipes, uncollected waste, and shortages of water-treatment chemicals created ideal conditions for the disease.

Thousands of people died, and tens of thousands were infected. The outbreak exposed the failure of basic public health systems and drew international alarm. Humanitarian organizations rushed to provide clean water, rehydration salts, treatment centers, and sanitation support, but their work was hampered by the scale of the emergency and the broader political environment.

## Hyperinflation and Economic Breakdown

Zimbabwe’s humanitarian crisis was inseparable from its economic collapse. In 2008, hyperinflation reached catastrophic levels, wiping out wages, savings, pensions, and the ability of ordinary people to buy basic goods. Prices changed several times a day, and people often carried huge bundles of banknotes that were nearly worthless.

The Zimbabwean dollar lost practical value, forcing many transactions into foreign currencies or barter. Shops were empty, fuel was scarce, and public transport became unreliable. Workers paid in local currency found that their salaries could not cover even a bus fare or a loaf of bread.

The government printed ever-larger denominations of currency, but this only deepened the collapse. Hyperinflation destroyed formal commerce and pushed many Zimbabweans into informal trading, cross-border buying and selling, or dependence on remittances from relatives abroad.

## Political Standoff and Violence

The humanitarian emergency unfolded during a deeply contested political period. In March 2008, Zimbabwe held presidential and parliamentary elections. The opposition MDC, led by Morgan Tsvangirai, made major gains, and Tsvangirai won more votes than Robert Mugabe in the first round of the presidential race, though official results said he had not secured enough to avoid a runoff.

The period that followed was marked by widespread political violence, intimidation, and arrests, particularly against opposition supporters. Tsvangirai withdrew from the June runoff, citing violence against his supporters, and Mugabe proceeded to claim victory in an election widely criticized by international observers.

The resulting political deadlock delayed a coordinated response to the worsening humanitarian situation. Regional leaders, especially through the Southern African Development Community (SADC), pushed for negotiations. These talks eventually led to a power-sharing agreement between ZANU-PF and the MDC, but implementation was slow and contested.

## Humanitarian Aid Under Pressure

Aid agencies played a crucial role in preventing an even greater catastrophe. They provided food assistance, emergency medical care, cholera treatment, nutritional support, and water and sanitation services. Yet their work was often difficult. Political suspicion, bureaucratic restrictions, poor infrastructure, fuel shortages, and insecurity limited access to affected communities.

At times, the government accused humanitarian organizations of supporting the opposition, while critics accused the authorities of obstructing aid for political reasons. This tension made it harder to reach vulnerable populations quickly and impartially.

## Regional and International Concern

Zimbabwe’s crisis had regional effects. Refugees and migrants crossed into South Africa, Botswana, Mozambique, and Zambia, seeking food, work, medical care, or safety. The cholera outbreak also crossed borders, increasing pressure on neighboring health systems.

International governments and organizations called for urgent humanitarian access, political reform, and economic stabilization. Many Western countries criticized Mugabe’s government for repression and mismanagement, while some African leaders favored quieter diplomacy. The crisis became both a humanitarian emergency and a major test of regional political mediation.

## Legacy of the 2008 Crisis

Zimbabwe’s 2008 crisis was not caused by a single event. It was the result of years of political conflict, economic mismanagement, weakened institutions, declining agricultural production, and deteriorating public services. By the end of the year, hunger, disease, and poverty had reached emergency levels.

The formation of a unity government in 2009 helped stabilize some aspects of the economy, especially after the abandonment of the Zimbabwean dollar in favor of foreign currencies. Food availability improved in some areas, and cholera was eventually brought under control. But the trauma of 2008 remained profound.

For many Zimbabweans, that year symbolized the collapse of the basic social contract: a time when money became worthless, hospitals stopped functioning, children went hungry, and political rivalry overshadowed human suffering. The crisis remains a stark reminder that humanitarian disasters are often intensified when economic failure, public health breakdown, and political deadlock occur together.

counterfactuals.output:
**Zimbabwe Faces Severe Shortages as Political Crisis Deepens**

*HARARE —* Zimbabwe is facing worsening shortages of food, fuel, medicine, cash and electricity, intensifying a humanitarian and economic crisis as a political dispute over a proposed unity government remains unresolved.

Long lines have formed at fuel stations and banks across the country, while many shops have empty shelves or prices beyond the reach of ordinary citizens. Hospitals and clinics are struggling with shortages of essential drugs and equipment, and power cuts have become frequent as the country’s electricity supply falters.

The crisis comes after years of economic decline under President Robert Mugabe, who has ruled Zimbabwe since independence in 1980. Critics blame his government’s policies, including the seizure of white-owned commercial farms beginning in 2000, for damaging agricultural production and undermining investor confidence. Mugabe and his allies say Western sanctions and external interference are responsible for the country’s problems.

Zimbabwe has also been hit by hyperinflation and a severe shortage of banknotes, leaving many people unable to withdraw cash or buy basic goods. Aid agencies have warned that millions of Zimbabweans need food assistance, particularly after poor harvests and the collapse of local production.

The political crisis deepened after a disputed presidential election. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai won the first round of voting but did not secure enough votes to avoid a runoff, according to official results. Tsvangirai withdrew from the runoff, citing violence against opposition supporters, and Mugabe was declared the winner in a vote widely condemned by Western governments and rights groups.

Under regional pressure, Mugabe’s ZANU-PF party and Tsvangirai’s Movement for Democratic Change agreed in principle to form a unity government. But negotiations have stalled over control of key ministries, especially the Home Affairs Ministry, which oversees the police. The MDC has accused Mugabe of attempting to retain effective control of the security apparatus, while ZANU-PF says the opposition is being influenced by foreign governments.

Western countries, including the United States and members of the European Union, have imposed targeted sanctions on Mugabe and senior officials, including travel bans and asset freezes. They say the measures are aimed at individuals accused of undermining democracy and human rights, not the broader population. Mugabe’s government says the sanctions have damaged the economy and should be lifted.

Regional leaders in the Southern African Development Community have urged both sides to implement the power-sharing agreement, warning that continued deadlock could worsen the suffering of ordinary Zimbabweans.

For many Zimbabweans, the political dispute has become secondary to daily survival. Residents in Harare and other cities say they spend hours searching for bread, cooking oil, fuel and cash, often relying on relatives abroad or informal markets where prices are far higher.

Analysts say any recovery will depend on a credible political settlement, restoration of agricultural output, renewed international assistance and stabilization of the currency. Until then, Zimbabwe’s shortages are expected to continue, deepening pressure on a population already battered by years of crisis.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article beginning “HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) --” about children wasting away in Zimbabwe due to food shortages, economic collapse, cholera, and political turmoil.
counterfactuals.output:
HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) -- In the dim corridors of an overcrowded clinic on the outskirts of Harare, mothers sit shoulder to shoulder with children too weak to cry. Some of the children have the telltale signs of severe malnutrition: thinning hair, swollen feet, skin stretched tightly over bones. Others stare blankly from beneath blankets, their small bodies weakened by hunger, diarrhea and disease.

Across Zimbabwe, health workers and aid agencies say a deepening humanitarian crisis is leaving thousands of children wasting away as food shortages, economic collapse, cholera outbreaks and prolonged political turmoil converge with devastating force.

“This is not just hunger,” said one nurse at a public health facility in the capital, who asked not to be named because she was not authorized to speak publicly. “These children are arriving with multiple problems — malnutrition, dehydration, infections. Their families have no food, no clean water and no money for transport to get help.”

Zimbabwe has faced years of economic instability, marked by soaring prices, high unemployment and shortages of basic goods. For many families, even staple foods such as maize meal, cooking oil and bread have become unaffordable or unavailable. In rural areas, poor harvests and erratic rainfall have compounded the crisis, while in urban neighborhoods, residents say wages no longer keep pace with daily costs.

Parents describe skipping meals so their children can eat, diluting porridge to make it last longer, or relying on wild fruits and handouts from neighbors. But for the youngest children, especially those under 5, prolonged food deprivation can quickly become life-threatening.

“My child used to run and play,” said a mother waiting outside a treatment room with her 2-year-old son wrapped in a faded towel. “Now he just sleeps. I came here because he stopped eating, but they told me he is very weak.”

Doctors say malnutrition leaves children vulnerable to diseases that would otherwise be treatable. Cholera, which spreads through contaminated water and poor sanitation, has hit communities already struggling with failing infrastructure. In some neighborhoods, residents line up for hours at boreholes because municipal water supplies are unreliable. Others use unsafe sources when clean water is unavailable.

Public health experts warn that cholera can kill within hours if untreated, particularly among children who are already weakened by hunger. Oral rehydration salts, intravenous fluids and antibiotics can save lives, but clinics often face shortages of medicine, clean supplies and staff.

Zimbabwe’s health system, once considered among the strongest in the region, has been battered by years of underfunding and the departure of skilled professionals seeking better pay abroad. Hospitals and clinics frequently lack essential equipment, and some patients are asked to provide their own bandages, gloves or medication.

Aid organizations are trying to scale up feeding programs and emergency health interventions, but workers say access, funding and logistics remain major challenges. Political tensions and administrative obstacles have also complicated relief efforts in some areas, according to humanitarian officials.

The country’s political turmoil has deepened public frustration, with critics accusing leaders of failing to address the basic needs of citizens. Government officials have at times blamed sanctions, drought and global economic pressures for the country’s difficulties, while opposition figures and civil society groups point to corruption, mismanagement and repression as key drivers of the collapse.

For families on the ground, the political debate feels distant compared with the daily struggle to survive.

In a crowded township market, vendors sell small piles of tomatoes, onions and grain at prices many shoppers cannot afford. A grandmother caring for four grandchildren said she buys food one day at a time, whenever she can scrape together enough cash.

“Sometimes we eat once,” she said. “Sometimes we drink tea and sleep.”

Nutrition specialists say the visible signs of wasting — extreme thinness, lethargy and stunted growth — reflect only part of the damage. Malnutrition in early childhood can impair brain development, weaken immunity and increase the risk of death from common illnesses. Even children who survive may face lifelong consequences.

At one clinic, a health worker measured the circumference of a toddler’s upper arm using a color-coded tape. The marker fell into the red zone, indicating severe acute malnutrition. The child’s mother looked down silently as staff prepared to admit him for treatment.

“We can stabilize some of them,” the nurse said. “But when they go home, what do they go back to? No food, no clean water, no sanitation. They come back again, worse than before.”

Humanitarian agencies have called for urgent support, including expanded food distribution, treatment for malnourished children, clean water provision and cholera prevention campaigns. They also warn that without broader economic and political stability, emergency aid can only blunt the worst effects.

For now, the crisis is measured in the bodies of children arriving at clinics — thinner each week, weaker each day — and in the desperation of parents who say they have run out of options.

“I just want him to live,” said the mother holding her son outside the treatment room. “If there was food at home, he would not be like this.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
